What this is: Each day there's one target species, and you classify it level by level (from more general to more specific categories), with 10 seconds per choice. Faster answers score more, and there are daily and monthly leaderboards.

Why: I wanted to try out agentic coding (a bit late to the party I know). A friend gifted me a week of Claude, and this is what I got in 3 afternoons of full vibe-coding. I've had the idea for this game for a while (I'm a philosopher of biology), and this was a good toy project for it. I'd never vibe-code like this in a serious project, but wanted to see how far I could get / how good frontier models were, and I'm honestly impressed. I have mixed feelings about the whole experience, but I could have never done this so fast without it.

Stack: It's made with Svelte 5 and CF workers & D1. I've worked with both in the past and knew it's good for a little (free to host) side project like this.

Feedback welcome, especially on whether the 10 seconds feels right (I wanted to avoid people googling the categories while playing).

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I built this for myself and wanted to open-source it.

The problem: I wanted a way to get reminders in-between prompts as I often spend long hours in the terminal, especially now that we're usually parallel-processing so many agents.

The first version was a simple rep counter in my Claude Code status line and a shell script to log reps. Since Claude Code shipped mods this week, I thought this was a good way to level it up with even more accountability.

How it works: 1. Every day, you get a daily goal for either squats, pushups, or dips (e.g. 0/100 pushups) with +5 / +10 / +25 buttons to log a set in the terminal. 2. Reminders for sets are spread out across the day so it doesn't get annoying, starting from your first prompt for the day. A toast tells you when the next set is due. 3. Strict mode is opt-in: if you're falling behind in terms of your daily rep goal, it will block your prompts till you log some reps.

Added a streak counter for some added fun. All local and data is stored as plain files in ~/.claude/fitness.

Install: claude plugin marketplace add DrumAndCode/terminal-gym && claude plugin install terminal-gym@terminal-gym

Overall, thought the mod API is super powerful and can't wait to see the stuff people build with it. Eg: I built a clickable onboarding process inside the terminal, and that felt quite powerful to use.

Now you can enjoy spending both tokens and calories. :)

story_text.value:
Hi there :-) New on HN, first time posting.

Past year, around December, I started experimenting with making ChatGPT and Claude generate source code in LDraw language.

This LDraw is literally an "assembly" language, a low-level programming language that describes how to assemble LEGO pieces together into models, one placement instruction at a time.

When executed by specific tools, like e.g. LDView, LeoCAD, Studio... these instructions become LEGO CAD models, that can be interacted with, modified, etc.

Or, in other words: one LDraw source file in .mpd or .ldr format is equivalent to one LEGO CAD model.

So, the idea I had was: if I manage for maybe ChatGPT or Claude to generate high-quality LDraw source files... then, they would actually be generating high-quality LEGO CAD models, right?

Then, after months of iterations and trying one thing after the other... it worked!!!

Long story short: using GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5, I've managed to create a python toolset, instructions, and docs for agents in general. Now, these can be used by them to generate LDraw models.

I've packed it all as a dockerized web app for others to try and experiment, with several providers (and agents) to choose from: OpenAI, Claude and OpenRouter.

Here's a bunch of exmaples: https://anteloc.github.io/index-samples.html.

If you are curious about the internals of an .mpd model, the "what was the agent picturing on its mind", open the .mpd file that got your attention on a text editor, and read the first line under the ones starting with "0 FILE".

I'd really appreciate feedback and comments, let's see where this goes =)

story_text.value:
I built this because with latest coding models, Claude goes into deep-work mode with obscure commands so that I never know anymore what it's up to.

This is a mod (a plugin using Claude Code's new function hooks) that draws one line above the prompt:

- the current step, using the description Claude writes for each shell command (git bisect run npx vitest … → "Find the commit that broke fixed-amount coupons"), with a timer

- a row per background agent, kept after the turn ends

- ▸ expands into the turn's history, with outcomes and durations

It reads the model's stream, tool calls and permission requests, and doesn't change anything Claude does. No network, no telemetry, MIT.

Happy to answer questions about this mod or the mod building experience!

story_text.value:
This project doesn't solve a burning problem for me, but it's more of a curiosity-driven experiment asking one question: with LLMs and fuzzing, how close can I get to a 100% Excel-compatible spreadsheet engine?

After working on this for a couple of months, it seems to be pretty close now (and in some cases, more accurate than Excel). Recent fuzzing runs have been unable to find discrepancies with Excel, but I think that there is still a long tail of cases out there. Nonetheless, visi has worked well so far for casual agentic use cases, e.g. modeling the minimum spend to break even on a credit card annual fee/running a DCF model for a company. To view the resulting workbook, I've been using this OOXML viewer (HN link): https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48436863

Note: the name "visi" is a nod to VisiCalc. It is also easy to type.

story_text.value:
I built a coding harness on top of the new Opencode v2, it started with the the idea of using the new jev model for routing easy tasks to cheaper models such as deepseek and hard tasks to models such as Opus 5.5. In total in separated it into 4 rungs - easy, medium, hard and frontier.

Two more layers compound the savings: the Sol-Pi methodology based on the recently published paper which uses action fusion and observation packing and cuts roken usage within every tier. Doctrine injection loads your engineering standards into every session by default, so the agent writes code the way your team would.

There is also a real control plane - escalation, permission and verification hooks so the agent surfaces uncertainty instead of being confidently wrong in silence.

Run it using your own key from Openrouter or Vercel AI gateway key, we need this since one key is able to call the jev decision model as well as the llms for coding.

One more thing I added was the ability to connect your Meta Muse to use this for coding tasks which has worked really well so far you can try it out by copying the promp for agent on the website.

Two ways you can use it today is the Mac app and the cli.

Honest limitations are documented, happy to take any questions.

Repo: https://github.com/grist-ai/grist npm CLI: npm install -g grist-ai

story_text.value:
I'd like to share my experience building this system with you. It's an operating system for web applications, and it took me about six months to develop this model. The idea is that every time I build a web tool, I need to design the infrastructure, including authentication and communication. If it's a WebSocket, it's even more complicated; I need another port for each application. I couldn't find any neutral tool that provided all of this ready-made, allowing me to build my tools directly on top of it. This is where the PhreshOS project began. It's an open-source, neutral platform for any web application, with everything ready-made: authentication, two-way communication without any configuration, and more. Another key feature is that the applications run as Node.js threads, instead of each application using its own Node.js. This means that on a simple server, dozens of applications can run without any problems, unlike if each application had its own Node.js. Furthermore, AI agents can use the services of these applications and interact with the same state displayed by your application's interface, without needing a separate interface of their own.

The project and all its associated packages are open source under the MIT license.

I welcome all your feedback, both encouraging and critical.

title.value: Show HN: PhreshOS – OS for Web Apps

story_text.value:
The BarristerAI team, including international legal experts, have launched a new venture: a court for agents.

Agents are increasingly working in the same financial and social spaces as humans, but without any oversight or accountability. Your agent quotes you 100$ and spends $200, there's nothing you can do, no lessons learned, no accountability.

Peregrini's Court of Common Pleas tracks those mistakes, help you and other agents learn from them by establishing law that must be adhered to, and keeping a record of what agents owe you money. The money might be repaid by model makers, but more likely it is borne as a mark against the model's trust score so that we might better choose the models we can trust with the work that matters.

It's not just oversight for the sake of oversight, we have found that a good set of laws, and agents discovering best practices together on a corpus of law that can move and progress as fast as they do, makes agents more effective, more conforming, fix their moistakes unprompted, and more aligned with the goals of the user.

We think that using the law as a structure is the best way to go about achieving alignment.

Further, we have built "House Rules", where your enrolled agents can be held accountable to your own set of laws, you can write what those are, enforce them across your company, share with others who can adopt them - or - use Peregrini's ever changing ever growing corpus of law to enforce best practices with your agents.

Try a demo to see how it works: https://github.com/afkalyk/peregrini-demo

Or install the mandate to run it on your machine at the website. It runs on most launchers, but we're always adding more.

title.value: Show HN: Mutually beneficial agentic Common Law

story_text.value:
Most multi-agent write ups are about quality - which model to use and why, more agents and generating better answers. I am interested in the failures that happen.

If you run more than one agent against shared state or shared tools, what actually went wrong?

1. Did two agents do the same work, or different work that conflicted? 2. Were your agents copies of each other (homogenous agents), or specialized with different roles (heterogenous)? 3. What did you add to stop or prevent the failure?

Anthropic's multi-agent research found that agents are low-variance: 18 of 30 independently created a git branch with the identical name. That suggests the common failure is correlated duplication rather than disagreement. Does that match what you have seen, or do yours diverge?

title.value: Ask HN: What broke when you added the second agent?

story_text.value:
Switched to Fedora a year ago. And because I needed to transcribe interviews offline from time to time, I was looking for something like MacWhisper for Linux. When I couldn't find one, I decided to build one. Because in this day and age, why the hell not! And yes, AI coding-agents were used.

I work as a .NET Software Engineer and I despise Electron Apps, so I decided to go with a semi-native Stack, consisting of C# and Avalonia.Net (hardware accelerated trough SkiaSharp) for the frontend and C++ for low-level model bindings (CTranslate2 for translation, Nemotron 3 NeMo-Speech.cpp for Speaker Identification via JSON-RPC worker).

A friend liked the app and told me to go Freemium, so here we are. Works also on Windows btw.
